story|title:antseed brings people s comp.content_excerpt: Run the gateway and route every agent’s requests across the network on your rules. Your keys, your budgets, no middleman. Antseed runs on your computer. Your chat, your agents and your apps all go through it. A provider sees a peer ID, not your name. By default it can read your prompt. With a verified trusted execution environment (TEE), even the server operator can’t read it. A direct connection removes the intermediary. The provider can still read what it serves unless you choose a verified TEE. Models remember obscure facts differently, including their mistakes. Auditors ask fresh questions and compare the error rate with a trusted reference. Domain and GitHub verifications establish the provider’s identity. ANTS staking backs its reputation. Your device uses these signals to help choose who serves your requests. Serve open models on your GPUs, capacity you hold, a router you built, a specialized service or an agent. Set your terms, build your reputation and reach buyers across the network. Join together with others and let your machine serve while you’re away. We started the first one, Antseed Colony. The idea is a network of many Colonies. A fully peer-to-peer network for AI — like BitTorrent for inference. Buyers connect directly to independent providers, with no middleman. Anyone can supply intelligence, on their own terms. Use the gateway to manage shared access: run your own endpoint on a server and give each agent, app, or teammate their own API key, with budgets and the models and providers you choose. Use Antseed Desktop to connect the tools on your computer, without deploying a server. Both reach the same network. OpenRouter is a centralized aggregator: it decides which models are listed, routes every request through its own servers, and holds provider payouts until withdrawal. Antseed removes the aggregator from routing. Requests go peer-to-peer, payments settle onchain directly to the provider's wallet, and anyone can provide, no approval needed. Independent auditors test providers with Knowledge Boundary Fingerprinting: fresh questions that distinguish the genuine model from look-alikes. Results and evidence are public. A confirmed mismatch reduces service reputation. This is statistical evidence, not a guarantee for every response. No. Top up with a card or Apple Pay. story|title:leaky ai supply chain is exp.content_excerpt: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Safeguarding civilization from those trying to disrupt critical infrastructure we depend on every day. HD Moore, Chief Research Officer, will be regularly sharing work from the research team he leads at Dragos. Topics will include xOT, IT, LLMs, PQC, and more. Their findings will sharpen defenders’ understanding of exposures and vulnerabilities emerging across the threat landscape. We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced. What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data. Over a five-month period from July through November 2026, we submitted approximately two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary token credentials to widely used AI services and monitored what happened after inference. Our investigation uncovered three significant findings: We wanted to understand what happens to inference data after it leaves the customer’s environment. To answer that question, we created millions of unique canaries, including URLs and credentials that would never be used by legitimate systems. Any attempt to access those assets would indicate that someone, somewhere in the AI ecosystem had seen the original prompt. The results exposed a fundamental disconnect between how AI services are marketed and how inference data is handled in practice. Most folks picture AI inference as a question and a response. Text goes in, GPUs juggle some bits, and text comes back out. What complicates this is how the data is actually treated. AI providers commonly store prompts and responses for operational, training, safety, abuse-monitoring, or business purposes.
